summary: A memory-ownership release: owned vectors are reclaimed at scope exits, and the UI text pipeline stops growing its per-frame footprint.

highlights.title: Owned vectors are freed at scope exit
highlights.text: Fresh and call-return vectors, match-bound result payloads, and aggregate fields are now reclaimed at loop, match, and function exits. Long-running editors and scripting workloads no longer grow without bound.

highlights.title: Text rendering stays flat
highlights.text: The font-shaping and glyph-raster wrappers declare caller-owned return buffers, and unsafe foreign calls no longer hide transient vectors from the drop pass. A 1,200-frame animated UI soak holds steady instead of reaching the memory cap.

highlights.title: Element access keeps vector ownership
highlights.text: Reading or writing a vector element no longer marks the whole vector as escaping, so per-iteration scratch vectors are reclaimed while taking an element reference still escapes.

highlights.title: UI builds link with the new allocator path
highlights.text: Main-heap allocations in ownership-contract functions use the C allocator directly, so UI applications link against older runtime objects and no longer fail with a linker error.

highlights.title: Owned return contracts for read helpers
highlights.text: io.read_file_bytes and io.read_at carry #[owns_return]: the Ok payload is a fresh main-heap Vec owned by the caller. Older pins ignore the attribute; the next compiler registers the payload for a scope-exit drop, removing the read-path Vec leak.

known_issues: An actually-taken retry in a function that rebinds an owned vector can leak only the replaced buffer; the returned buffer is still caller-owned.
Microcontroller targets use a bump allocator and do not support exceptions; vendor peripherals are not emulated.
